title: Trump: Rep. Sessions, son of Mogilevich attorney, stalls Russian sanctions bill
description_short: Trump: Rep. Sessions, son of Mogilevich attorney, stalls Russian sanctions bill
description_medium: Representative Pete Sessions sought to delay a Russia-sanctions bill in the House in June 2017 after it had passed the Senate with overwhelming support. The linked account describes his objections to provisions he said could disadvantage American energy companies. The legislation also required congressional review before the president could loosen specified sanctions.
description_long: On June 29, 2017, Representative Pete Sessions sought to slow a Russia-sanctions bill that had passed the Senate with broad support. The legislation would require congressional approval before the president could remove or alter specified sanctions. Sessions objected to provisions he said could disadvantage American energy companies. The Trump administration also pressed lawmakers to change the measure, which constrained presidential discretion over sanctions. Pete Sessions's father, William Sessions, worked as an attorney and lobbyist for Russian businessman Semion Mogilevich. The family relationship formed part of the public context around the congressman's position, but does not by itself show that Mogilevich influenced it. Congress ultimately passed a revised bill, which Trump signed in August 2017. The episode was an effort to delay or alter the bill, not to prevent its enactment. The immediate legislative dispute centered on the balance between executive authority, congressional oversight and the effect of sanctions on U.S. businesses.

title: Trump: Chad Wolf, DHS block Intel warning about Russian smear campaign
description_short: Trump: Chad Wolf, DHS block Intel warning about Russian smear campaign
description_medium: DHS officials held back an intelligence bulletin warning of Russian efforts to attack presidential candidates' health and mental fitness in July 2020. The linked account says the draft was submitted for review on July 7 and scheduled for distribution to law-enforcement partners on July 9. It was not intended as a public media release.
description_long: In July 2020, the Department of Homeland Security held back an intelligence bulletin warning law-enforcement partners about Russian efforts to portray presidential candidates as mentally unfit. The draft, titled “Russia Likely to Promote Claims of Compromised Mental Health of US Presidential Candidates,” was submitted for review on July 7 and scheduled for distribution two days later. Chief of staff John Gountanis instructed staff to consult acting secretary Chad Wolf before release. Brian Murphy, then a senior intelligence official, later alleged that Wolf objected because the assessment would make President Trump look bad. Murphy said he challenged political interference with a vetted intelligence product and was excluded from later discussions. The dispute concerned a bulletin intended for law-enforcement partners, not a public media release. It raised questions about whether political considerations delayed a warning about foreign influence operations. The withholding kept the warning from law-enforcement partners on its planned distribution date. Murphy's later complaint placed the dispute in a broader debate about political interference in intelligence assessments during the 2020 campaign.

title: Trump's Pennsylvania election lawsuit moves closer to the Supreme Court
description_short: Trump's Pennsylvania election lawsuit moves closer to the Supreme Court
description_medium: The Third Circuit expedited consideration of a Trump campaign challenge to Pennsylvania's election certification in November 2020. The linked account says the district court had dismissed the case for inadequate legal arguments and unsupported accusations. The appeal sought review of a challenge with potentially sweeping effects on the state's voters.
description_long: In November 2020, the Third Circuit expedited its review of a Trump campaign lawsuit seeking to stop Pennsylvania from certifying its election result. The challenge followed U.S. District Judge Matthew Brann's dismissal of the case, which he criticized as a poorly assembled argument unsupported by evidence. The campaign's requested relief could have prevented certification and affected nearly seven million votes. The appeals court later unanimously rejected the challenge. Judge Stephanos Bibas wrote that serious allegations require specific claims and proof, and the campaign had not established a legal basis to overturn the state's result. Expedited scheduling only moved the appeal quickly; it did not signal that the judges accepted its claims. The appellate decision rejected the campaign's request to intervene in Pennsylvania's certification process and left the state's result intact. It also reinforced the requirement that election challenges present specific legal claims supported by evidence.
